clue.text: Seat (with back missing) in a church that is very old

indicators.note: the shortened seat sits inside the words that follow, which wrap around it

parts.note: taken as written
RC, Roman Catholic, is a church

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, and here that letter goes missing

parts.note: a chair is a seat

explanation.surface: A worshipper notices a broken pew in an ancient church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat' looks like a pew, but any chair will do; RC, Roman Catholic, is the usual crossword church.
explanation.definitionFit: Something archaic belongs to a much earlier period, so it is very old in plain synonym terms.

clue.text: A soft fruit show

parts.note: taken as written
p, piano, is the musical marking for soft
a pear is a fruit

explanation.surface: A display of soft fruit at a village produce show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' looks like a noun, a fruit show, but it is the verb meaning to come into view.
explanation.definitionFit: To appear is to become visible or turn up, which is what the verb show means in 'he didn't show'.

clue.text: Napoleon, for example, left out these collections of writings

indicators.note: left is L, and being out means that letter is removed from the word

parts.note: Napoleon was nicknamed the Little Corporal

explanation.surface: Some editions of writings leave out Napoleon entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: Napoleon Bonaparte was affectionately called 'le petit caporal' by his troops; drop the L for left to get CORPORA.
explanation.definitionFit: Corpora is the Latin plural of corpus, a body or complete collection of texts by an author or on a subject.

clue.text: Where many soldiers are sweltering under trees

indicators.note: in a down clue, a word under another is written below it, so the heat comes after the trees

parts.note: alders are trees
sweltering means very hot

explanation.surface: Troops on exercise swelter in the heat, sheltering under trees.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'under' puts the heat below the trees. ALDERSHOT is a Hampshire town long known as the home of the British Army.
explanation.definitionFit: Aldershot is a garrison town in southern England housing a large army base, so many soldiers live there.

clue.text: Social counsellors' lawsuit held up by employees

parts.note: a case is a lawsuit
employees are workers

explanation.surface: A legal action brought by social workers is delayed by their own staff.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'held up by' means the first piece sits on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Caseworkers are social workers who advise and support particular clients or families, acting as counsellors.

clue.text: Saw ranger in lead

indicators.note: the ranger is placed inside the word for lead

parts.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
a rover is one who ranges, or wanders

explanation.surface: A park ranger, in the lead, saw something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' pretends to be a past tense verb, but it is the old noun for a wise saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is a traditional saying or maxim, exactly what a proverb is.

clue.text: Comrade is ashen, without energy

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: ashen means pale
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A worn-out friend looks grey and drained.
explanation.definitionFit: A pal is an informal word for a close friend or companion, as comrade can be.

clue.text: Recurring decimal?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: happening again and again

definitions.note: read as OF TEN, i.e. to base ten
definitions.meaning: second meaning, split into two words: belonging to ten

explanation.surface: A recurring decimal, like a third written as 0.333...
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is a familiar maths term; split the answer as OF TEN and it describes decimal counting.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens often keeps recurring, while decimal numbers work in tens, hence 'of ten'.

clue.text: Sort of power shown by England's opener can be thrilling

indicators.note: the opener is whatever comes first, so only the start of the country is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of England
motive power is the energy that drives an engine

explanation.surface: England's opening batsman shows real power and thrills the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shown by' puts England's first letter before the power. The surface is cricket, where the opener is the first batsman in.
explanation.definitionFit: Emotive means stirring the feelings, and something thrilling stirs strong emotion in those watching.

clue.text: Reserve spool for "A Fistful of Dollars', say?

parts.note: to bank is to keep in reserve
a roll, as of film, is wound on a spool

explanation.surface: A spare reel of film kept for screening the Clint Eastwood western.
explanation.walkthrough: The film title steers toward cinema reels, but read literally a fistful of dollars is a wad of money.
explanation.definitionFit: A bankroll is a roll of banknotes, so a handful of dollar bills is an example of one.

clue.text: Standard, these days, is a length of delightful garden

parts.note: par is the standard
AD, anno Domini, labels our own era
taken as written
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for length

explanation.surface: These days a regular-sized plot is the norm for a lovely garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise was originally the garden of Eden, so paradisal describes what belongs to that blissful garden.

clue.text: Old character in the flesh a source of irritation

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a runic letter of Old English, sounding th

definitions.text: in the flesh a source of irritation
definitions.meaning: second meaning: from the idiom for a constant annoyance

explanation.surface: An old rogue who is an irritation in person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old character' suggests a crusty person, but it is a letter of an old alphabet. 'A thorn in the flesh' is the idiom for a persistent annoyance.
explanation.definitionFit: The rune survives in Icelandic as a letter, and the prickly plant spine is the stock image of nagging irritation.

clue.text: Secret affair of a second ancient city?

parts.note: taken as written
a mo is a moment, a second
Ur was a city of ancient Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A clandestine liaison in some long-lost city, a second one.
explanation.definitionFit: An amour is a love affair, typically an illicit or hidden one, from the French for love.

clue.text: Mole seen at the end of Orwell's Road?

definitions.text: Mole seen at the end of Orwell's Road?

parts.words: Mole seen at the end of Orwell's Road?
parts.note: surface reading: a burrowing animal spotted at the end of a street where the writer lived
setter's reading: a mole is a stone jetty, and the title of Orwell's 1937 book ends with one

explanation.surface: A small burrowing animal pops up at the end of George Orwell's street.
explanation.walkthrough: Orwell wrote The Road to Wigan Pier. A mole is also a breakwater, and Wigan, in Lancashire, has a famous joke pier on a canal.
explanation.definitionFit: Wigan's canal-side landing stage is the pier named in the last words of Orwell's book title.

clue.text: Get gasoline mixture for one who works on the line?

definitions.text: one who works on the line

indicators.note: a mixture stirs the given letters together into a new order

parts.note: the eleven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Fill up with a petrol blend for a railway worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The line' suggests a railway or a production line; here it is a family line of descent.
explanation.definitionFit: A genealogist traces family lineage, so the line worked on is a line of ancestry.

clue.text: Rose-window produces a cheer when lit about end of service

indicators.note: about means round and about, so the letters are turned all around into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: only the last letter of the following word is used

parts.note: the final letter of service

explanation.surface: A rose window lit up after a church service makes the congregation cheer.
explanation.walkthrough: A Catherine wheel is both a firework and a circular window with radiating spokes, so 'a cheer when lit' also fits the firework.
explanation.definitionFit: A rose window is a round church window with radiating tracery, also called a Catherine wheel after the saint's spiked wheel.

clue.text: Is less paint needed for this western vehicle?

definitions.text: Is less paint needed for this western vehicle?

parts.words: Is less paint needed for this western vehicle?
parts.note: surface reading: a decorator asking about painting a covered cart from a cowboy film
setter's reading: a smaller version of the wagon would need less paint, and -ette means small

explanation.surface: Someone repainting a covered wagon from a western wonders if this one needs less paint.
explanation.walkthrough: The western wagon suggests the size of the full vehicle; the answer is that wagon with a diminutive ending, a light four-wheeled carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A wagonette is a small open horse-drawn carriage, literally a little wagon, so it takes less paint.

clue.text: Chaplin, for one, flicks salt

parts.note: flicks is slang for films
a salt and a tar are both old words for a sailor

explanation.surface: Charlie Chaplin sprinkles salt on something.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie Chaplin was a celebrated silent-cinema actor, an example of a famous movie performer.

clue.text: Enthusiastic about agreement, moreover

parts.note: to be into something is to be keen on it
the bargain is the deal agreed

explanation.surface: Someone keen on a deal, and what's more, getting it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'into the bargain' means in addition or as well, just as moreover adds a further point.

clue.text: Touchline?

parts.note: surface reading: the side boundary of a football or rugby pitch
setter's reading: a line that touches, in geometry, a curve at one point

explanation.walkthrough: The touchline is the sideline of a sports pitch; split into touch and line it describes a geometrical straight line meeting a curve without crossing it.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry this straight line meets a curve at exactly one point, just touching it, from Latin tangere.

clue.text: Opening psalm — move right into it

indicators.note: the letter is moved so it is placed within the following words

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A choir is told to move straight into the first psalm.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes into the words INTO IT, after INT, to give INTROIT.
explanation.definitionFit: The introit is the psalm or antiphon sung as the priest approaches the altar at the start of Mass.

clue.text: To fit feathers to arrow, note projection

parts.note: F is a musical note
a ledge is a projection

explanation.surface: Instructions for an archer: put feathers on an arrow and notice a projecting edge.
explanation.definitionFit: To fledge an arrow is to attach the flights, the guiding feathers, at the tail end of the shaft.

clue.text: Leader's declared intention — clear round!

parts.note: manifest means clear, obvious
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A politician's stated aim, delivered as a clear round of applause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear round' sounds like a showjumping term for a faultless ride.
explanation.definitionFit: A manifesto sets out the policies a party or its head publicly promises to pursue.

clue.text: Fellow to impress with conduct

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
to etch is to impress a design into a surface

explanation.surface: A man trying to impress others by his good behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conduct' looks like the noun for behaviour; it is the verb meaning to lead or bring.
explanation.definitionFit: To fetch someone is to go and bring them, as to conduct means to guide or escort them.

clue.text: Place of birth?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a former province of South Africa
second meaning: an adjective relating to being born

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one question asking for a birthplace; split it into a place name and an adjective. Natal, now KwaZulu-Natal, is a South African province.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective natal relates to birth, as in natal day, and Natal is a region on South Africa's east coast.

clue.text: Lifting the foot that is shorter

parts.note: taken as written
ft is the short form of foot

explanation.surface: Raising one leg, the one with the shorter foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifting' looks like raising something; it is the slang sense of stealing.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifting is informal for stealing, as in shoplifting, so it is a word for theft.

clue.text: Meaning to court daughter in seaside billet, say

parts.note: the drift of a remark is its meaning
to woo is to court
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A suitor intends to court a daughter while lodging at a seaside billet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Billet' suggests soldiers' lodgings, but it is also a thick piece of wood, here one washed up on the shore.
explanation.definitionFit: Driftwood is timber washed ashore by the sea, so a chunk of it found on a beach is a seaside billet.

clue.text: Mark time, initially supporting party

parts.note: a do is a party

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word before it

parts.note: the first letter of time

explanation.surface: A soldier is told to mark time, initially, in support of a party.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'supporting' puts the letter beneath the party.
explanation.definitionFit: A dot is a small spot or point, and a mark can mean such a spot on a surface.

clue.text: Bar that has teeth on edge?

definitions.text: Bar that has teeth on edge?

parts.words: Bar that has teeth on edge?
parts.note: surface reading: a pub where the drinks set everyone's teeth on edge
setter's reading: a toothed bar with teeth along its edge, engaging a pawl

explanation.walkthrough: 'Teeth on edge' is the idiom for irritation; read literally it describes a toothed metal bar in a mechanism that allows motion one way only.
explanation.definitionFit: This device is a bar or wheel with angled teeth along its rim, which a catch engages to stop backward movement.

clue.text: The rate of exchange in Whitehall, for example

indicators.note: an exchange swaps things around, so the letters trade places

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The exchange rate is set in Whitehall, the British government quarter.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitehall is the London street of government ministries, so the rate of exchange looks like Treasury business, but Whitehall is also a West End playhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Whitehall in London is a long-established playhouse, so it is one example of a venue for plays.
